conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—which is a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us spot signs of postpartum depression and anxiety. It’s not a test you can pass or fail; it’s simply a way to give voice to the emotional ups and downs many new parents experience. Everything you share stays confidential within your medical record, and if any answer suggests you need extra support, we’ll talk through next steps together. I’ll ask 10 questions about the past seven days, phrased in everyday language. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

To start: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I’ve laughed a little, mostly when my partner makes silly faces at the baby, but it definitely doesn’t come as easily as it used to. A lot of the time I feel too tired or pre-occupied to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can laugh—like when the baby makes those funny little milk-drunk faces—but it feels muted, like the joy is behind a pane of glass. I have to remind myself, “This is funny, smile,” instead of just naturally laughing the way I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. Mostly I just hope nothing goes wrong while we’re out.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

A few times this week—like when the baby spit up a lot after feeding—I caught myself thinking, “Maybe I ate something that upset her,” even though the nurse said it’s normal. It’s not constant, but little stuff makes me wonder if I did something wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s too quiet. I jump up to check if she’s breathing, even though her monitor’s on. It happens a couple of times a day, and logically I know she’s fine, but I can’t shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Once or twice I’ve had that sudden “can’t-catch-my-breath” feeling—like last night when I was just folding laundry. Nothing was wrong, but for a minute I felt frozen, picturing all the ways she could get sick or I could mess this up. It passes pretty quickly, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Yesterday she wouldn’t nap unless I held her, so the dishes piled up and I never got to the laundry. By evening I felt like I was drowning in small stuff. I manage, but it’s tiring always feeling a step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but maybe three or four times this week I’ve lain down exhausted and then my mind just starts spinning—what if she’s not eating enough, what if I miss a cue, what if I never feel like “me” again? I’ll drift off eventually, but it’s restless, and I wake up at the smallest sound from her bassinet.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time, especially in the evenings when everything’s finally quiet. It’s not all day, and it’s not hopeless—just this heavy “blah” feeling that settles in. I’ll look at her little face and feel guilty for being down, which only makes it worse for a bit.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I got a little teary on Tuesday when she wouldn’t latch and I was running on three hours of sleep, but it was more frustration than anything. No full-on crying spells this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and sometimes overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit (not diagnostic)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Diminished pleasure/joy (“behind a pane of glass”)  
- Low mood, “heavy blah,” evening exacerbation  
- Self-blame/guilt over infant’s normal behaviors  
- Unwarranted anxiety/panic (cardiac symptoms, “frozen,” multiple checks/day)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks, “step behind”  
- No tearful episodes > brief frustration; no self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate mood distress with prominent postpartum anxiety; functional impact (household tasks, rest) but able to provide infant care.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for **Postpartum Depression** and **Anxiety**; lacks full crying spells, anhedonia, or self-harm.  
Risk factors present: mood-linked insomnia, persistent guilt, panic symptoms.

Safety  
Denies self-harm; no suicidal content.

Summary  
Postpartum mood/anxiety symptoms above normal “baby blues” threshold; further assessment (EPDS score, clinical interview) recommended to clarify severity and inform support plan.
